query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In corrosion‐resistant steels used for chemical processing and nuclear power, the exceptional corrosion resistance arises from the rapid formation of a chromium‐rich passive film that is promoted by enhanced grain boundary density. This leads to selective Fe dissolution and preferential Cr oxidation, which, in turn, forms a stable, protective barrier in aggressive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional duplex or stainless steel with nominal Cr and Ni contents exhibiting a coarse-grained microstructure and uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply a processing route (such as severe plastic deformation or controlled heat treatment) to refine the grain size, thereby increasing the density of grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Exposure to simulated aggressive environments, for example, chloride-containing aqueous solutions at ambient to moderate temperatures (chemical-processing conditions) and high-temperature, molten salt or high-temperature water environments (nuclear power conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary density that accelerates the selective dissolution of more active elements (like Fe) and facilitates the enrichment of Cr at the surface and grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The finer microstructure increases the area of high-energy grain boundaries, which preferentially promotes the oxidation of Cr over Fe. This leads to faster formation of a continuous, chromium-rich passive film that acts as an effective barrier against further corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a coarse-grained baseline, the processed (fine-grained) steel will display a more rapidly forming and thicker Cr-enriched passive film, resulting in a lower corrosion current density and improved overall corrosion resistance under identical environmental exposures.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained stainless steel with standard Cr distribution and passive film formation kinetics.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for steels with sufficient Cr content when exposed to moderately aggressive aqueous and high-temperature corrosive environments, but may not apply if the Cr content falls below a critical threshold or under extreme (e.g., highly acidic or oxidizing) conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of grain refinement versus inherent alloy composition to the rate and stability of passive film formation are not precisely determined; moreover, potential interactions with other alloying elements (e.g., Ni, Mo) may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless steel samples with the same chemical composition and Cr content: one set with a conventional coarse-grained microstructure and another set processed by severe plastic deformation to produce an ultrafine-grained structure. Expose both sets to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution at a fixed temperature) and, in a separate study, to a simulated high-temperature molten salt environment. Use identical exposure times and environmental conditions.
measurements: Electrochemical polarization tests to measure corrosion current density and potential.
Surface analysis via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or scanning Kelvin probe (SKP) to quantify the Cr content in the passive film.
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to confirm grain size and passive film morphology.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not exhibit significantly enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film and do not show a statistically lower corrosion rate compared to the coarse-grained samples under both test conditions, then the hypothesis—that grain boundary–mediated Cr enrichment is the governing cause of the improved corrosion resistance—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
